title: Longest common subsequence: subsequence enumeration vs dynamic programming
problem_statement: Given strings a and b, compute the length of the longest string that is a subsequence of both.

input.parameter: n = length of each string (|a| = |b| = n in the harness).

algorithms.name: subsequence enumeration
algorithms.idea: Enumerate all 2^n subsequences of a and test each against b with one greedy scan.
algorithms.pseudocode: for each subset S of positions of a: if a[S] is a subsequence of b: best = max(best, |S|)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(2^n n) on every input with |a| = |b| = n (n >= 1): each mask costs between n and 2n steps, counting the characters that b.find examines (the upper bound under the machine-model assumption in background that str.find scans forward and stops at the first match)
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n) with the input; beyond it O(1) values (mask, scan position, flag, best)
algorithms.correctness: Exhaustive; the greedy leftmost-match scan decides the subsequence relation exactly (PROOFS.md sections 1-2).

algorithms.name: dynamic programming
algorithms.idea: L(i, j) = L(i-1, j-1) + 1 if a_i = b_j, else max(L(i-1, j), L(i, j-1)); fill the table row by row.
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2): exactly |a| |b| inner iterations and |a| + 1 rows of length |b| + 1 (Theta(|a| |b|) for non-empty strings)
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n): at most two rows of length |b| + 1 beyond the input
algorithms.correctness: Optimal substructure of LCS on prefixes (PROOFS.md section 2; credit: CLRS).

relationship: Exponential enumeration of candidate subsequences is replaced by a quadratic table of prefix-pair subproblems. Proofs of every claim: PROOFS.md.

sources.authors: Cormen, T. H.; Leiserson, C. E.; Rivest, R. L.; Stein, C.
sources.title: Introduction to Algorithms (3rd ed.)

sources.authors: Wagner, R. A.; Fischer, M. J.
sources.title: The string-to-string correction problem

sources.authors: Abboud, A.; Backurs, A.; Vassilevska Williams, V.
sources.title: Quadratic-Time Hardness of LCS and other Sequence Similarity Measures
CPython source code: Objects/stringlib/fastsearch.h
sources.note: Background only (machine-model assumption). Read on 2026-10-07 (main branch): a search for a one-character needle calls find_char, which scans forward from the start (memchr for long strings) and returns the first index of the character, or -1.

verification.method: V1: both agree on random DNA-alphabet string pairs (n <= 12 for enumeration). V2: runtimes fitted against 2^n n and n^2 (measurements, not proofs). Proofs: PROOFS.md proves every claim of the entry (correctness of both algorithms, time and space); tests/test_proofs_lcs.py checks the computable facts on stated ranges, including both outputs against an oracle that intersects the sets of all subsequences.

caveats: The conditional lower bound from the literature is background (cited, not proved here); see background.

lower_bounds.bound: no O(n^(2-eps)) algorithm for any eps > 0
lower_bounds.setting: conditional on the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH)
lower_bounds.source: Abboud, Backurs & Vassilevska Williams 2015, main result (background: cited, conditional, not proved in this entry)

background.statement: An O(n^(2-epsilon)) algorithm, for some epsilon > 0, for the LCS of two sequences of length n would refute the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH).
background.source: Abboud, Backurs & Vassilevska Williams 2015 (FOCS 2015; arXiv:1501.07053), main result as stated in the abstract

background.statement: Machine-model assumption of this entry: str.find(c, j) with a one-character c scans the string forward from position j and stops at the first occurrence of c (CPython's find_char: a forward loop, or memchr on long strings), so it costs O(1) plus the number of positions it examines. Read off the CPython source; not proved in this repository.
background.source: Python Software Foundation, CPython source Objects/stringlib/fastsearch.h (find_char), read 2026-10-07
